accuracy.evidence: Every comparison was checked by hand: 1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4 > 1/5, 4/5 > 2/5, 5/8 > 3/8, 1/3 > 1/6, 3/7 < 5/7, 1/4 < 1/2. The parameterised items use a*(a>b)+b*(b>a) style answers with a!=b, so the expected numerator or denominator is always the larger or smaller one, and the cake item keeps a greater than b.

misconceptions.evidence: Names the classic whole-number bias recorded by Ryan and Williams and by Hansen: a bigger denominator 'looks' bigger, so 1/5 is called more than 1/3. It also covers 'both are fifths so they are equal', flipping the < and > signs, and comparing halves and quarters of wholes that are not the same size.

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagfcmp lab is new: a slider that recuts one bar into 2 to 12 parts while leaving ghost bars of earlier cuts, a tap-to-order queue of unit fractions, shading pairs of fifths and eighths, a tap-to-cycle sign gap and a drag of a pizza slice onto a different-size pizza. None of these mechanics appear in the tenths or fraction-bar labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The steps follow the NCETM sequence: first see that more equal parts make smaller parts, then order unit fractions, then compare fractions with the same denominator by counting parts, then write the result with < and >, and finally learn that the comparison only holds for the same whole. The challenge mixes all of these.

predictions.evidence: Four predict prompts come first: what happens to each part when the same bar is cut into more parts, which of 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 is biggest, whether 2/5 or 4/5 is bigger, and whether Mia's half of a small pizza beats Leo's quarter of a giant one. The options include the whole-number-bias answer so the bar or pizza then shows the result.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions send wrong answers through a why() helper that names the slip, such as 'A bigger denominator means more parts, so each part is smaller', 'Same denominator means same-size parts, not same fraction' and 'That is smallest first'. Right answers restate the rule, and the lab moves on only after a correct tap.

readability.evidence: Kid text is about Flesch-Kincaid grade 1.7, using the curriculum words numerator, denominator, greater than and less than, each explained in one short sentence. The adult text is about grade 7.9, quotes the Year 3 statement and 3.NF.A.3d exactly, and lists the common errors so a parent knows what to watch for.

no_filler.evidence: There are no stock openers or wrap-up phrases. Each kid paragraph introduces one idea with a worked pair of fractions, and each adult paragraph has a standard, a rule, a list of errors or a description of the lab. The content gate's filler and overlap checks passed.

mobile.evidence: Phone screenshots at 390 px show the bar, ghost bars, order slots, shading bars and pizzas fitting the frame. Fraction cards, shading cells, sign buttons and the slider thumb are large tap targets, and the pizza slice can be dragged or placed with a button, so a child never needs fine aim.

accessibility.evidence: The canvas has an aria-label set for each step, fraction buttons carry spoken labels such as 'one third', feedback goes to a polite live region, and axe found no violations in light or dark themes. Size is shown by bar length and by the numbers themselves, not by colour alone.
